2.text: However, no Chukchee has patience enough to cut six feet of ice, as the

3.text: Russianized fisherman of the Kolyma does in setting his net.

4.text: Bag-nets fastened to a square frame made of thin stakes (Fig. 63) are

5.text: used in shallow water. The vertical stakes of the frame have

6.text: sharp points, and are driven into the ground.

7.text: The ice-scoop used by the Chukchee (Fig. 64) is of the

8.text: well-known Eskimo form, chiefly of small size, and has a cir-

9.text: cular hoop of antler netted across with whalebone strings or

10.text: thin strips of leather. A round hoop-net made of whalebone

11.text: (Fig. 65), with one large stone beneath for a sinker, is used for

12.text: catching wachna.¹ It is identical with the American Eskimo net.²

13.text: Nordenskiöld³ gives a picture of a fish-spear made of bone.

14.text: On the Pacific coast I met with the fish-spear only among the Kerek

15.text: near Cape Anannon, and in several places among the Kam-

16.text: chatka Koryak. Their spears, however, are more or less similar

17.text: to that given by Nordenskiöld. The specimen represented in

18.text: Fig. 66 probably formed one of the prongs of a fish-spear.⁴
